slides.text: Data Centres in Ireland. Why are we talking so much about it?
Every time you stream a video, send an email, or ask a question to an AI, a server, somewhere has to do the work. That server sits in a data centre.
slides.footer: It requires electricity to run, water to cool down, material to build ... a lot of it. This is why it matters.

slides.caption: In fact, it is estimated that 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions already come from our digital lives, more than aviation. It is growing fast as AI takes off. which requires more data centres to be built.

And Ireland has a lot of them. In fact, Ireland hosts around 25% of all European Data Centres. Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, they all built major operations here. Dublin has quietly become Europe's data capital.
And powering those data centres consumed 22% of Ireland's entire electricity in 2025, up from almost nothing a decade ago.
slides.footer: For context, Ireland's entire peak national demand tops out at around 6,000 MW, and prospective new data centres are already requesting up to 5,800 MW.

slides.text: Is this a problem? This debate looks very different depending on where you are.
bullets: Iceland runs data centres on geothermal power. Not much concern there.
The UK has a diverse grid, a very different balance. Right now the main concern is more around water consumption.
slides.footer: Ireland's grid on the other hand is still partly fossil-fuelled. Every new data centre is a direct competitor for green energy that was meant to decarbonise homes and factories.

slides.text: Since 2015, nearly all growth in Ireland's electricity demand has come from data centres. The wind farms we're building aren't replacing fossil fuels — they're just keeping up with new AI demand.
slides.footer: Between 2020 and 2023, only 16% of increased data centre demand was matched by new renewable purchases. The rest came from the standard grid mix, keeping us dependent on gas and coal.

slides.text: Ireland's grid is so strained that regulators have imposed a de facto moratorium on new connections in Dublin. New data centres must now build their own power generation or batteries before they can connect.
slides.footer: Because renewable energy is intermittent, many are turning to on-site gas turbines. Decarbonisation, meet the bypass.

slides.caption: New power demand for data centres is not just an Irish problem. It is projected to grow by 165% by 2030. AI will be a big part of it.
slides.footer: But as AI becomes more efficient, shouldn't energy demand be less?

slides.text: When a technology becomes more efficient, total consumption goes up, not down. This is known as the Jevons Paradox
slides.footer: Cheaper AI means more AI, everywhere. More efficient chips don't lower the electricity bill — they make it possible to build bigger, more powerful systems that were previously too expensive to run.

slides.caption: But it's not all negative. Digital transformation and AI will have a significant positive impact in reducing emissions — up to 15-20% reduction in global greenhouse gas emissions according to the World Economic Forum.
slides.footer: AI can optimise grids, model climate systems, cut industrial waste, and accelerate clean energy. The same technology stressing Ireland's grid could also help save it.

slides.text: The question is not whether Ireland should have data centres. It is whether we are setting the right terms.
slides.footer: Mandatory renewable energy requirements, community benefit agreements, water impact rules, and smarter location choices could make the difference between a tech boom that helps the energy transition, and one that derails it.
